overview: The union of Great Britain and Ireland began in 1801, replacing Ireland’s separate Parliament with representation at Westminster. During its nineteenth-century height the state built railways, mills and a global empire, while Irish famine, colonial violence, unequal suffrage and dangerous city housing exposed the costs of that power. Campaigns over schooling, toilets and voting reshaped daily life. Most of Ireland became the Irish Free State in 1922; the formal royal and parliamentary title changed in 1927, before this map’s 1938 endpoint.

periods.title: Union, industry and abolition
periods.summary: Ireland entered the UK in 1801. Cotton mills and railways grew as Parliament ended British slave trading in 1807 and slavery in most colonies under the 1833 act.

periods.title: City growth and Irish catastrophe
periods.summary: Industrial cities offered work but often unhealthy housing. Potato failure, poverty and policy combined in the Irish Great Famine, driving death and emigration.

periods.title: Public health and school reform
periods.summary: New public toilets appeared unevenly; school boards grew in England and Wales, with different Scottish arrangements. Children’s access still depended on income and place.

periods.title: An empire and demands for representation
periods.summary: The state ruled territories across the world while people there contested colonial control. At home, campaigners demanded votes and Irish self-government.

periods.title: War, wider voting and Irish independence
periods.summary: World war reshaped civilian work and food. The 1918 franchise widened but remained unequal for women. War and negotiation in Ireland led to partition and the Irish Free State in 1922.

periods.title: A changed union and formal title
periods.summary: Northern Ireland remained in the UK after most of Ireland separated. In 1927 the royal and parliamentary title was amended to reflect Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

periods.title: Beyond the old title
periods.summary: The UK continued with a changed formal name and territory. This map record’s 1938 end should not be read as a second political collapse.

items.text: The 1801 union joined Great Britain and Ireland in one UK. The Irish Parliament ended, but political demands from Ireland did not. Saying “the UK ruled Ireland” alone misses that Ireland was formally inside this union and fiercely debated its terms.

British factories drew cotton from an Atlantic world shaped by slavery. Parliament barred British slave trading in 1807 and legislated abolition of slavery in most colonies in 1833. Owners received compensation; formerly enslaved people did not. Legal reform did not erase colonial inequality.

The empire extended across continents, but its colonies were homes to peoples with their own laws, labor, resistance and aims. Parliamentary empire milestones record both British expansion and later independence; they are not a list of places that simply waited to be ruled.

Most of Ireland became the Irish Free State in 1922 after treaty and conflict; Northern Ireland remained in the UK. The 1927 title changed to Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Those were political transformations, not the disappearance of Irish or British families.

Manchester cotton mills and the 1830 Liverpool to Manchester Railway represented spectacular engineering, but mill families worked amid noise, strict hours and crowded housing. Ancoats excavations even found a domino: workers still made moments for games.

In 1831 more than half of houses in one Manchester district, Ancoats, lacked plumbing when cholera spread. This is a neighborhood measure, not a figure for every British home. A family’s risk of disease could depend as much on a pipe as on a doctor.

The 1870 law helped local school boards build classrooms in England and Wales; Scotland passed its own school law in 1872. In 1880 five-to-ten-year-olds had to attend, yet many children still worked outside lessons or missed school because their wages mattered at home.

In 1851 a visitor at the Great Exhibition paid a penny for a public toilet. Victorian towns gradually built more, but facilities for women were especially scarce. A family outing could require planning around something as ordinary as a bathroom break.

The Irish Great Famine from 1845 to 1852 killed many and pushed many more to leave their homes. Families experienced hunger and separation within the same state that displayed industrial power. Blight mattered, but so did unequal resources and the government response.

sections.title: War, votes and a written name

items.text: First World War rules reached into homes through blackouts, air-raid precautions and food rationing. Women entered jobs long labeled “men’s work,” while family care and grief continued. Not all women had the same opportunity or pay.

In 1918 most adult men and some women over 30 gained voting rights, with a property rule for those women. Equal voting age at 21 came in 1928, after this card’s formal name had changed. A law called “reform” could still leave many neighbors outside the ballot box.

The 1800 union statute names “The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.” This short written English title is an original-language sample from official text; Irish, Welsh, Scottish Gaelic and other languages also belonged to residents’ lives.

A map segment carries this old formal name as far as 1938. The Irish Free State began in 1922, and the title had changed by 1927. The polygon endpoint is imported coverage, so it cannot certify that the earlier title remained current until 1938.

ending.text: After most of Ireland became the Irish Free State in 1922, Northern Ireland remained in the UK. In 1927 Parliament adjusted the royal and parliamentary title to Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The UK continued; its old full title changed. The imported map segment runs to 1938 and must not be treated as the date of a second independence or state ending.
